# Storage Engine & Gateway Specification

## 1. Executive Summary & Overview

The Knowledge Substrate (TKS) manages software engineering system evolution through governed requirement topologies.
Modern software systems suffer from intent drift and architectural degradation when autonomous agents execute code changes without explicit grounding in verified architectural contracts.
This specification defines the foundational storage architecture, protocol gateway boundaries, persistent relational schemas, and operational execution tasks necessary to implement the Knowledge Substrate.
The system provides bidirectional traceability between high-level architectural requirements, concrete implementation tasks, and source code artifacts.
By anchoring development workflows to a unified property graph stored within a relational database, engineering teams can maintain rigorous supervisory oversight while enabling autonomous agent execution loops.
In complex enterprise environments, requirements frequently diverge from running code due to fractured communication channels, out-of-band pull requests, and undocumented engineering decisions.
The Knowledge Substrate eliminates this divergence by formalizing requirements as first-class, navigable property graph nodes directly integrated into continuous development pipelines.

## 2. System Architecture & Topology

The Knowledge Substrate architecture is structured as a layered, modular system composed of three primary operational tiers:
First, the Stateless Protocol Gateway exposes Model Context Protocol (MCP) and REST endpoints to client environments, developer tools, and external autonomous coding agents.
Second, the Storage Core manages relational graph topology, dense vector embeddings, Git document ledgers, and forensic audit event sequences within a single unified PostgreSQL database.
Third, the Background Worker Pool executes asynchronous document decomposition, local vector embedding inference, and scheduled maintenance tasks.

```text
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
       |             External Autonomous Agents & Tools              |
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
                                      |
                                      v
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
       |                  Stateless Protocol Gateway                 |
       |             (Model Context Protocol & REST API)             |
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
                                      |
                                      v
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
       |                         Storage Core                        |
       |       (Relational Graph, Audit Ledger, Git ODB Actor)       |
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
                                      |
                                      v
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
       |                     PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector                |
       +-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### 2.1 Component Separation & Responsibilities

Each component operates under strict isolation boundaries to ensure predictable performance and deterministic fault domains.
The gateway layer never executes internal agent cognitive loops and maintains zero long-lived in-memory session state.
Every client request contains complete authentication credentials and executes as an isolated database transaction.
The background worker pool operates independently of client gateway threads, utilizing dedicated connection pools to prevent request latency degradation.
Administrative operations and schema migrations execute through embedded migration harnesses before the network listener binds to incoming ports.
System telemetry, structured logging, and distributed tracing propagate request identifiers across all asynchronous boundaries, providing end-to-end visibility into substrate operations.

### 2.2 Relational Schema & Storage Engine

All relational graph topology, vector representations, document source spans, and audit records reside in a single PostgreSQL 16+ instance.
The primary tables include:

- `graph_nodes`: Stores requirements, specifications, tasks, decisions, and verification rubrics with 0-based source span offsets.
- `graph_edges`: Represents typed, directed topological relationships between nodes, including structural lineage, constraints, and fulfillment edges.
- `node_embeddings`: Manages 384-dimensional dense vector embeddings generated by local CPU runtimes, consolidated with status state machines.
- `audit_ledger`: Implements an immutable, append-only event ledger tracking all approved mutations with monotonically increasing integer sequence numbers.
- `ingestion_jobs`: Coordinates asynchronous document decomposition pipelines across staging, approval, and promotion states.
- `agent_identities`: Authenticates human supervisors and external agent instances through cryptographic token hashes and role assignments.

### 2.3 Concurrency Control & Advisory Locking

To guarantee topological consistency and prevent cycle creation in the active requirement Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG),
all structural edge mutations, draft batch promotions, and administrative rollbacks acquire a global transactional advisory lock.
This advisory lock is acquired prior to any row-level locking, ensuring complete serialization of topological validations across concurrent sessions.
Read-only queries, including micro-reflex context envelope traversals and full-text keyword searches, execute concurrently without acquiring advisory locks.
Lock contention is minimized by ensuring that mutation transactions execute in bounded time without performing external network calls or heavy computational processing while holding locks.

### 2.4 Vector Search Integration & HNSW Indexing

Vector similarity search allows external agents and human supervisors to discover semantically related requirements even when exact terminology differs.
The substrate employs dense vector embeddings generated by lightweight embedding models operating on commodity CPU hardware.
Embeddings are indexed using Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs configured with cosine distance operator classes.
To optimize index maintenance and prevent index corruption from unapproved drafts, the HNSW index is restricted strictly to active nodes with completed embeddings.
Queue polling and background embedding workers process pending embedding records asynchronously without blocking interactive ingestion or staging approval workflows.

### 2.5 Audit Ledger Monotonic Event Sequencing & Historical Reconstructibility

Every approved mutation to the active requirement graph creates an immutable audit event in the `audit_ledger` table.
The ledger utilizes an identity column sequence generating strictly monotonic 64-bit integer values (`event_seq`), guaranteeing an unambiguous total ordering of all state transitions.
Each audit record captures pre-mutation snapshots, post-mutation snapshots, atomic transaction correlation identifiers (`batch_id`), and originating actor identity fingerprints.
This immutable ledger enables point-in-time state reconstruction, deterministic undo operations, and administrative rollbacks without data loss or historical ambiguity.
Draft entities and exploratory agent proposals reside in an isolated draft lifecycle, preventing speculative agent churn from bloating the canonical audit ledger.

### 2.6 Document Provenance & Exact 0-Based Byte Span Coordinates

Requirements extracted from unstructured technical markdown documents maintain strict provenance links to the originating document artifact.
Rather than storing redundant text copies in disparate database tables, the substrate embeds 0-based byte offsets (`byte_start`, `byte_end`), document paths (`doc_path`), and cryptographic content hashes (`doc_hash`) directly as first-class columns on `graph_nodes`.
Zero-copy byte slicing extracts verbatim requirement text directly from buffered source bytes in memory, validating UTF-8 character boundary safety before string construction.
This design eliminates relational join overhead, prevents multi-row Cartesian product anomalies, and guarantees that extracted requirements can be verified against immutable document baselines at any time.

### 2.7 Model Context Protocol (MCP) Message Schemas & Tool Definitions

The Integration Gateway implements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification over standard input/output (stdio) and Server-Sent Events (SSE) transports.
The substrate exposes focused, deterministic tools allowing external agents to query context envelopes, search requirements, and propose candidate mutations:

- `get_context_envelope`: Assembles bounded topological subgraphs around a target requirement or task, incorporating ancestral constraints and immediate sibling rules.
- `query_requirements`: Performs hybrid retrieval combining PostgreSQL full-text keyword search and vector neighborhood ranking.
- `propose_node_mutation`: Allows authorized external agents to submit candidate requirements or tasks for staging review or autonomous elaboration.
Tool responses return structured JSON envelopes optimized for LLM token economy, avoiding redundant schema boilerplate and minimizing agent context window consumption.

### 2.8 Error Handling Hierarchy & Resilience Guarantees

All substrate internal APIs and gateway endpoints implement a standardized error reporting hierarchy.
Errors are categorized into client-recoverable validation errors (HTTP 400), authentication failures (HTTP 401), authorization policy denials (HTTP 403), resource non-existence (HTTP 404), concurrency conflicts (HTTP 409), and internal system faults (HTTP 500).
Database connectivity interruptions trigger automatic connection pool reconnection loops with exponential backoff and jitter.
Background workers catch internal panics within individual task scopes, recording failure diagnostics in job tracking tables without crashing the host process.

## 3. Normative Requirements & Invariants

### REQ-AUTH-01: Authentication Protocol

All inbound requests to the Integration Gateway MUST present a valid cryptographically signed bearer token.
Requests lacking valid credentials SHALL be rejected immediately with HTTP 401 Unauthorized.

### REQ-AUDIT-02: Forensic Audit Immutability

Destructive in-place updates on active requirements, specifications, and topological edges MUST NOT occur.
Every approved state mutation SHALL be recorded as a discrete, reversible event in the audit ledger.

### REQ-GRAPH-03: Upward Traceability Invariant

Every active functional specification and implementation task MUST maintain an unbroken upward directed edge path to an active requirement root.
Orphan execution tasks SHALL NOT be permitted in the active graph topology.

### REQ-ISOL-04: Draft Lifecycle Isolation

Candidate requirements and exploratory agent mutations MUST be stored with lifecycle state DRAFT.
Draft entities SHALL be caller-scoped and isolated from production agent context envelopes until approved.

### REQ-VEC-05: Fixed Dimension Vector Storage

All requirement vector embeddings MUST specify fixed dimensionality of 384 dimensions matching the reference model.
Dense vector indexing SHALL utilize partial HNSW cosine distance indexes restricted to completed embeddings.

### REQ-LOCK-06: Global Advisory Locking

Any transaction that mutates active graph topology or approves draft batches MUST acquire a global advisory lock.
Lock acquisition SHALL precede any row-level locks to prevent deadlocks across concurrent sessions.

### REQ-SPAN-07: Byte Span Coordinates

Every requirement derived through the decomposition pipeline MUST store 0-based byte span coordinates.
Span extraction SHALL verify character boundary safety before committing source span offsets.

### REQ-GOV-08: Per-Node Governance Authority

Permissions to alter or elaborate a graph node MUST be governed by explicit per-node governance policies.
Node policies SHALL take absolute precedence over global agent roles.

### REQ-IDENT-09: Agent Attribution

Every mutation submitted through the gateway MUST be attributable to a verified identity.
Unauthenticated or anonymous mutations SHALL be rejected at the gateway boundary.

### REQ-PERF-10: Traversal Latency

Micro-reflex graph traversal queries MUST execute in less than 50 milliseconds for up to 3 hops.
Context envelope assembly queries SHALL complete in less than 100 milliseconds.

## 4. Implementation Tasks

### TASK-MIGRATE-01: Execute Database Migrations

Run pending schema migrations against the PostgreSQL container using the embedded migration harness.
Verify that all tables, indexes, and constraints are cleanly established.

### TASK-DECOMPOSE-02: Implement AST Parser

Construct the streaming CommonMark AST parser using pulldown-cmark.
Implement active heading stack tracking to emit upward structural hierarchy edges.

### TASK-EVAL-03: Build Extraction Evaluation Harness

Implement precision and recall evaluation runner comparing candidate extractions against hand-labeled fixtures.
Measure token consumption ratio ensuring generated output tokens represent less than 10% of document input tokens.

### TASK-VECTOR-04: Benchmark CPU Vector Inference

Evaluate local embedding generation using fastembed and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on commodity CPU hardware.
Measure inference latency across batches of 1, 8, and 32 requirement chunks.

### TASK-SEED-05: Seed Developer Token

Insert the well-known development token into agent identities for offline and local testing.
Verify that the token is active and granted appropriate developer permissions.

## 5. Non-Normative Guidelines & Future Considerations

System operators should periodically inspect database index bloat and vacuum statistics.
Developers are encouraged to author clear, atomic specification blocks to facilitate automated decomposition.
In future iterations, additional embedding models and multi-lingual parsers may be evaluated.
When authoring technical specifications, markdown formatting should adhere strictly to standard CommonMark conventions.
Special attention should be directed toward maintaining consistent section hierarchy and avoiding deeply nested unparented lists.
Regular performance profiling of topological graph queries should be performed against realistic enterprise-scale datasets.
Database replication and read-replica offloading patterns should be established before deploying production instances to cloud environments.
Automated integration test suites should validate migration idempotency on every release candidate.
Security audits must review identity token hashing algorithms and verify proper credential rotation policies.
Document provenance tracking should be validated across successive Git commits to prevent span offset drift.
Continuous integration pipelines should incorporate linting, formatting, security scanning, and benchmark regression gates to maintain repository quality.
Architectural decision records must accompany all significant schema alterations, structural edge additions, or interface contract modifications.
Subsystem boundaries should remain decoupled through explicit interface contracts to allow independent horizontal scaling of gateway and worker nodes.
Telemetry collection should observe strict privacy policies, sanitizing sensitive authorization credentials and payload tokens before emission.
Performance benchmarks should establish latency baselines across commodity developer workstations and cloud virtualized hardware configurations.

## 6. Security Architecture & Threat Modeling

The Knowledge Substrate operates as a trusted coordination substrate within an organization's engineering ecosystem.
Because the substrate manages authoritative architectural contracts and directs autonomous coding agents, protecting the integrity of graph nodes and audit ledgers is paramount.
Threat analysis identifies several potential attack vectors that the substrate mitigates through defense-in-depth principles:
First, unauthorized mutation attempts by rogue or compromised agent processes are thwarted by per-node governance policies.
Even if an agent obtains valid API credentials, the gateway enforces node-level permissions, preventing agents from altering nodes governed by human review.
Second, prompt injection attacks embedded within third-party specifications cannot execute code within the substrate boundary because the storage engine never runs autonomous cognitive loops.
All inputs are parsed strictly into structured relational records and validated against strongly typed schemas before persistence.
Third, timing attacks against identity verification are mitigated by utilizing constant-time comparison algorithms during token hash validation.
Fourth, network interception risks are addressed by mandating Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3) for all remote gateway connections, with mutual TLS recommended for cross-datacenter deployments.
Audit records provide tamper-evident forensic history, ensuring that every state modification can be attributed to a specific verified identity and cryptographically verified against historical baselines.

## 7. Storage Engine Internals & Relational Topology

The underlying persistence architecture relies exclusively on PostgreSQL 16+ to minimize operational complexity and eliminate multi-database synchronization overhead.
The substrate models technical systems as property graphs using relational foreign key constraints and recursive Common Table Expressions (CTEs).
Nodes represent discrete engineering concepts, such as architectural requirements, structural invariants, behavioral constraints, interface specifications, implementation tasks, and verification rubrics.
Edges represent directed relationships connecting nodes into an acyclic dependency graph.
Lineage edges indicate which parent specifications give rise to child requirements.
Constraint edges define boundary rules that restrict how downstream components and execution tasks may be authored.
Fulfillment edges trace completed code artifacts and test suites back to their governing requirement roots.
By indexing foreign keys with covering composite indexes and utilizing partial indexes filtered on active lifecycle states, PostgreSQL executes multi-hop graph traversals with sub-millisecond latency.
Database maintenance procedures include automated autovacuum tuning, transaction ID wraparound monitoring, and index bloat mitigation.
Connection pooling via deadpool-postgres ensures that transient spikes in client query volume do not exhaust database backend processes or degrade query response times.

## 8. Asynchronous Processing & Background Worker Lifecycles

Background workers handle tasks that are either computationally intensive or decoupled from client request lifecycles.
Document decomposition, semantic vector generation, scheduled integrity audits, and dead draft reclamation all run within the worker pool.
Workers are managed by a centralized supervision daemon running on the Tokio asynchronous runtime.
Jobs are enqueued in relational status tables and polled using atomic database transactions (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`), preventing duplicate execution across concurrent worker processes.
Worker tasks execute within bounded timeouts and implement exponential backoff retry policies for transient failures.
When external API calls fail or credentials are not supplied, workers degrade gracefully by applying deterministic mechanical heuristics and committing draft entities with default typing.
Health check probes monitor worker loop progress and restart stalled actors automatically.
Worker resource consumption is capped through bounded channel buffers, preventing unbounded memory growth during high-volume ingestion batches.

## 9. Observability, Telemetry & Distributed Tracing

Comprehensive observability is essential for operating the Knowledge Substrate in production and diagnosing complex multi-agent workflows.
The system emits structured log events formatted according to standard JSON schemas, writing diagnostics strictly to standard error (stderr) to preserve standard output (stdout) for CLI tool protocols.
Log levels are dynamically configurable via environment filters, allowing operators to increase verbosity for targeted subsystems during troubleshooting.
Metrics collection tracks key operational indicators, including gateway request throughput, average query latency, database connection pool saturation, vector embedding inference duration, and cache hit ratios.
Distributed tracing instruments every incoming gateway transaction with a unique correlation identifier, threading trace contexts through background worker tasks and audit events.
Supervisory dashboards visualize graph topology statistics, tracking active requirement counts, pending draft volumes, and topological gap densities across engineering repositories.

## 10. Operational Runbooks & Deployment Guidelines

Deploying the Knowledge Substrate into production requires adherence to established infrastructure guidelines.
The recommended containerized topology deploys the compiled Rust binary alongside a managed PostgreSQL 16+ instance provisioned with high-speed persistent storage volumes.
Database volumes should utilize solid-state drives (SSDs) with adequate IOPS to support concurrent vector similarity lookups and transaction log writes.
Database parameters such as `shared_buffers`, `effective_cache_size`, `work_mem`, and `maintenance_work_mem` should be configured based on available host memory.
Automated backup runbooks mandate daily full physical database backups supplemented by continuous write-ahead log (WAL) archiving to cloud object storage.
Disaster recovery exercises should periodically validate point-in-time recovery to guarantee recovery point objectives (RPO) and recovery time objectives (RTO).
Rolling updates to substrate binaries must execute database schema migrations prior to traffic cutover, ensuring forward and backward schema compatibility.
In the event of an operational incident, operators can inspect the audit ledger to trace recent graph modifications, identify originating actors, and execute transactional rollbacks to restore known-good topological baselines.
